###### **Line** 

3-45. A _line formation_ is a movement formation in which elements move abreast of each other (FM 3-90). When assaulting a weakly defended objective, crossing open areas, or occupying an SBF position, the platoon mainly uses the line formation (see figure 3-3 on page 76). The platoon can use the line formation to maximize the platoon’s firepower and shock effect. The platoon normally uses the line formation when no terrain remains between it and the enemy, when the platoon has already suppressed the enemy’s AT weapons, or when the platoon is vulnerable to artillery fire and must move fast. Platoons typically only use the line formation when overwatched by another element. The line formation— 

- Is more difficult to control. 

- Permits maximum fires to the front or rear and minimum fires to the flanks. 

- Is less secure than other formations because of the lack of depth. 

- Can be slower to transition to other formations, depending on terrain.

###### **Wedge** 

3-46. The _wedge formation_ is a movement formation with one lead element and the trail elements are paired off abreast of each other on the flanks (FM 3-90). The platoon uses the wedge formation when the enemy situation is unclear or contact is possible, or the enemy situation is unclear. In this formation, the platoon leader and the platoon sergeant are in the center of the formation, with the remaining Strykers located to the rear of and outside of them. The wedge formation is a good formation for maintaining all-around observation and security. The wedge formation can be heavy left or heavy right (see figure 3-4), the platoon leader determines the formation based on likely enemy contact and terrain. The wedge formation— 

- Permits excellent fires to the front and good fires to the flanks. 

- Is easy to control. 

- Provides good security to the flanks. 

- Can be used with the traveling and traveling overwatch techniques. 

- Allows rapid transition to bounding overwatch.

###### **Echelon** 

3-47. An _echelon formation_ is a movement formation with elements arranged on an angle to the left or to the right of the direction of attack (echelon left, echelon right) (FM 3-90). When the company wants to maintain security or observation of one flank, and when the platoon does not expect enemy contact, the platoon uses the echelon formation (see figure 3-5 on page 78). The echelon formation is used to maximize fires in one direction, towards a flank. Typically used to cover an exposed flank of a larger force and when the platoon leader wants to maintain a high volume of fires without masking other elements. Unless there is another formation opposite the echelon, there is a risk of an exposed flank. The echelon formation— 

- Is difficult to control. 

- Affords excellent security for the higher formation in the direction of the echelon. 

- Facilitates deployment to the echelon flank.

###### **Vee** 

3-48. A _vee formation_ is a movement formation with two elements abreast and one or more elements trailing (FM 3-90). If there are more elements after the trail element in the vee formation, the trail elements can be in front or behind the main body. This arrangement is suited for an advance against a known threat to the front. The vee formation (see figure 3-6) is used when they know the enemy force’s location and disposition and expect enemy contact. The vee provides maximum firepower forward and good firepower to the flanks, but the firepower on the flanks is less than that provided by the wedge. The vee formation also allows a platoon to change quickly to a line, wedge, or column formation. The vee formation— 

- Is very effective at transitioning into traveling overwatch or bounding overwatch. 

- Is difficult to control in restricted terrain and under limited-visibility conditions. 

- Is more difficult to reorient the direction of movement. 

- Lead element may mask the fires of the trail element.

###### **Coil and Herringbone** 

3-49. The coil and herringbone are platoon-level formations employed when stationary and must maintain 360-degree security. The platoon may execute a coil or herringbone alone or as part of a company. Typically, per SOP, if a platoon stops in a security formation for more than a directed amount of time, it should start increasing security posture, such as CBRN monitoring, camouflage, sector sketches, and so on. Platoons should consider using Infantry to clear the area prior to moving vehicles off a road or trail. Platoons should always be aware of mines, improvised explosive devices, and other explosive hazards during movement. 

###### **_Coil_** 

3-50. The coil (see figure 3-7 on page 80) provides all-round security and observation when the platoon is stationary. It is useful for tactical refueling, resupply, and issuing platoon orders. Security is posted to include air guards and dismounted fire teams. The

The platoon repositions the vehicles as needed to take advantage of the best cover, concealment, and fields of fire. Fire team members dismount and establish security. ##### **FORMATION SELECTION** 

3-52. The platoon leader selects the formation that provides the proper security, direct fires, control, and speed for the operation. The platoon leader’s use of planned and rehearsed movement formations allows the platoon to rapidly shift from one formation to another, giving additional flexibility when adjusting to changes in mission variables. Rifle squads will operate with or without Stryker support while clearing terrain during movement. Stryker elements will provide overwatch while rifle squads clear terrain. The company commander may dictate platoon movement formations as part of the company movement. To ensure the effectiveness of the movement, platoon leaders must rehearse so that they can change formations using standard responses to changing situations. By designating the movement formation planned for use, the platoon leader— 

- Establishes the known relationship between units. 

- Indicates probable reactions once the formation makes contact with the enemy. 

- Indicates the level of security desired. 

- Establishes the orientation of platoon weapon systems. 

- Postures friendly forces for the attack. 

3-53. During rehearsals of movement formations, the platoon leaders should train Stryker elements to change formations on command, either by vehicle radio or using hand and arm signals. Stryker elements should be trained on each position in the selected formation, understanding weapons orientation and sectors of fire while moving. Platoon leaders and VCs must rehearse changing formations and fully understand their Stryker’s purpose in each type of formation. Moving from wedge to column or column to line is a difficult task and only happens if Stryker elements are trained and proficient in each type of movement formation. 

##### **MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES** 

3-54. Movement techniques limit the unit’s exposure to enemy fire and posture the unit to react to enemy contact. The platoon leader selects the appropriate movement 

**24 June 2025** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**81** 

**Chapter 3** 

technique based on the chance of enemy contact. Essential to the platoon selection of a movement technique is, first, understanding the company’s movement technique and movement formation, and second, understanding what element is in overwatch of the platoon. When contact is likely, but there is no external overwatch, the platoon leader must ensure there is overwatch within the platoon. While moving, individual Soldiers and mounted elements use the terrain to protect themselves when enemy contact is possible or expected. They use natural cover and concealment to avoid enemy fires. Soldiers and mounted elements— 

- Take active countermeasures, such as using obscuration, direct and indirect fire, to suppress or obscure suspected enemy positions. 

- Cross open areas quickly and avoid large open areas, especially areas surrounded by high ground or terrain that can cover and conceal enemy forces. 

- Avoid possible kill zones because it is easier to cross difficult terrain than to fight enemy forces on unfavorable ground. 

- Do not silhouette themselves against the skyline. 

- Do not move directly forward from a concealed firing position. 

- Ensure the lead element clears terrain past the intervisibility line, so the main body does not become decisively engaged. 

3-55. Movement techniques are not fixed formations. They refer to the distances between Soldiers, teams, and squads, mounted elements, and vary based on mission, enemy, terrain, visibility, and other factors affecting control (see table 3-2). The platoon leader uses the movement formations in conjunction with movement techniques. There are three movement techniques: traveling, traveling overwatch, and bounding overwatch. An _overwatch_ is a task that positions an element to support the movement of another element with immediate fire (ATP 3-21.10). The platoon leader selects from these movement techniques based on— 

- The likelihood of enemy contact. 

- The type of contact expected. 

- The availability of an overwatch element. 

- The level of security required during movement. 

- The timeline of higher headquarters. 

3-56. The selection of a movement technique is based on the likelihood of enemy contact and need for speed. Factors to consider for each technique are control, dispersion, speed, and security.

##### **DISMOUNTED MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES** 

3-57. Stryker Infantry rifle platoons and squads normally move mounted until the situation requires them to dismount. Once dismounted, fire teams usually move in wedge formations, and the platoon or squad uses one of the three movement techniques based on the likelihood of enemy contact. (See ATP 3-21.8 for more information on dismounted movement techniques.) 

##### **MOUNTED MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES** 

3-58. The Stryker platoon leader bases their decision on which movement technique to use based on the enemy situation. As the probability of enemy contact increases, the platoon leader adjusts the movement technique to provide greater security. Digitized and limited-visibility equipment provide the leader with a clearer update of the situation. Based on the most recent update, the leader executes either the traveling, traveling overwatch, or bounding movement technique. For example, if the platoon leader receives an enemy update from higher headquarters showing the enemy much closer to the platoon than originally anticipated, they immediately switch from the traveling to the bounding technique. 

3-59. The platoon leader selects from the three movement techniques (see figure 3-9) based on several factors: 

- Likelihood of enemy contact. 

- Type of contact expected. 

- Availability of an overwatch element. 

- Level of security required during movement. 

- Timeline of higher headquarters. 



**Figure 3-9. Transition from movement techniques to maneuver** 

###### **Traveling** 

3-60. _Traveling_ is a movement technique used when speed is necessary and contact with enemy forces is not likely (FM 3-90). The platoon leader is located where they can best control the situation. All elements of the unit move simultaneously. Trailing elements

###### **Traveling Overwatch** 

3-61. _Traveling overwatch_ is a movement technique used when contact with enemy forces is possible (FM 3-90). Traveling overwatch is an extended form of traveling that provides additional security when speed is desirable, but contact is likely (see figure 3-11 on page 86). The vee formation lends itself very well to traveling overwatch. The leader of the formation designates one of their subordinate elements to provide security forward of the main body. The security element may increase its distances from the main body because of improved enemy and friendly situational information. The trailing element moves at variable speeds and may pause for short periods to overwatch the lead element. The trailing element controls its movement based on the terrain and position of lead element. The rear element overwatches at such a distance that if enemy forces engage the lead element, it will not prevent the rear element from firing or moving to support the lead element. Leaders track the movement of and use position updates to ensure the forward security element is on azimuth and does not exceed the range of supporting direct fires. Likewise, the security element leader confirms their location and direction using navigation systems. Should a break in contact occur, the— 

- Leader or detached element uses navigations aids to reestablish contact with the main body. 

- Platoon’s main body uses an infrared (IR) or thermal source to regain visual contact with the element and link it back up with the main body.

###### **Bounding Overwatch** 

3-62. _Bounding overwatch_ is a movement technique used when contact with enemy forces is expected (FM 3-90). The leader initiates bounding overwatch based on planning information received earlier from the enemy situation and SITREPs received during movement. When contact is expected, the platoon dismounts the Infantry squads. DPs should be pre-planned based on the enemy situation.

###### **_Combined Mounted and Dismounted_** 

3-63. The mounted element moves by bounds in support of the dismounted Infantry. Depending on the terrain (visibility), a mounted element may overwatch one or two squads as they bound forward while the other mounted element(s) overwatch the remaining squad(s) (see figure 3-12). The dismounted Infantry will move forward or to the flanks of the mounted element(s). The mounted element halts and occupies overwatch positions to enable the dismounted Infantry freedom of maneuver. The mounted element maintains continuous visual contact with the bounding Infantry. If visual contact is lost, the mounted element should maneuver to re-establish visual contact as soon as possible. While IR and digital technology enable the platoon leader observation and control beyond organic direct fire weapon range, the bounding dismounted Infantry should not exceed the supporting mounted element's weapons planning range. The overwatching mounted element continuously re-positions itself to support the moving dismounted element by fire and maneuver. Dismounted Infantry continue to clear the terrain while the mounted elements enable freedom of maneuver by providing SBF. The mounted element(s) bounds forward at the pace of the dismounted Infantry, while maintaining visual contact. As a technique, the mounted element may be ordered to bound past the dismounted Infantry to provide direct fires in support of the dismounted Infantry, but caution should be taken as the mounted element is susceptible to enemy antiarmor. 

**_Note._** The designated mounted leader will direct and control the maneuver of the mounted element in support of dismounted operations, provide overwatch, call for fire, and serve as a communications relay.

###### **_Mounted_** 

3-64. The mounted element moves by bounds. One element always halts in position to overwatch another element while it moves. If the bounding element is out of visual contact after reaching the overwatch position, it signals that it is ready to overwatch using voice communications or a visual signal. The overwatching element positions itself to support the moving element by fire and maneuver. The platoon leader must not allow the bounding element to exceed the weapons range of the supporting element even though IR and digital technology allows the leader to observe and control movement beyond the range of their organic direct fire weapons. (See figure 3-13.) 



**Figure 3-13. Bounding overwatch, mounted** 

3-65. There are two variations of the bounding overwatch technique: alternating bounds and successive bounds. In both cases, the overwatch element is assigned sectors to scan while the bounding element uses terrain to achieve cover and concealment. Infantry squads should clear intervisibility lines and defiles prior to the Strykers occupying overwatch positions. The overwatching mounted element can immediately support the bounding elements, both mounted and Infantry squads, with fire or maneuver against the enemy if the bounding elements makes contact. Unless they make contact en route, the bounding elements move via covered and concealed routes into the next set of SBF positions. The platoon leader uses the terrain, available cover, and the available supporting range of overwatching weapons to determine the length of bounds. The platoon leader can use the uncommitted part of their forces whenever needed as part of an immediate and controlled reaction to any threat to the bounding force. In the absence 

**24 June 2025** 

**88** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**Offense** 

of suitable positions from which to overwatch, the platoon should move in traveling overwatch. 

###### **_Alternating Bounds_** 

3-66. If the platoon uses alternating bounds (see figure 3-14 on page 90), the bounding element moves forward, halts, and occupies an SBF position. The stationary element always covers the bounding element’s movement, halt, and occupation of the bounding element’s SBF position. The bounding element advances past the stationary element, takes an overwatch position, and becomes the new forward element. The former stationary element now becomes the bounding element, advances past the stationary element, and occupies a new SBF position. This method is usually more rapid than successive bounds. 

###### **_Successive Bounds_** 

3-67. As depicted in figure 3-14 on page 90, if the unit uses successive bounds, the lead element, covered by the trail element, advances, and occupies an SBF position. The rear element advances to an SBF position abreast of the lead element and halts. The lead element moves to the next position and the move continues. Only one element moves at a time, and the rear element avoids advancing beyond the lead element. Successive bounds are an effective technique that deconflicts movement with direct fires. For instance, leading with the left-side Stryker element allows clear fires to the front and front-right.

###### **_Clearing Defiles_** 

3-68. In geography, a defile is a narrow pass or gorge between mountains or hills which could force vehicles to move in a column with a narrow front. Using dismounted Infantry is integral to providing security while clearing a defile and transition from movement to maneuver. Dismounting the Infantry may slow down the tempo, but it is necessary to survive first contact. Critical to establishing tempo, platoon leaders ensure the dismounted and mounted forces synchronize their movements to be mutually supporting. One technique for accomplishing synchronization is for the platoon to rehearse bounding overwatch dismounted, mounted, and combined. Clearing a defile can be understood as a deliberate and planned variation of the bounding overwatch movement technique. When conducted correctly, the dismounted Infantry move ahead or to the flanks of the mounted elements and clear defile locations. 

3-69. Platoons must plan for and allow time and space for dismounted Infantry to approach and clear terrain. Platoons can use obscuration fires or terrain to deny the enemy observation and dismount the Infantry closer to defiles. _Deny_ is a task to hinder or prevent the enemy from using terrain, space, personnel, supplies, or facilities (ATP 3-21.20). The platoon leader may use UASs to conduct initial reconnaissance of known defiles. When the dismounted Infantry approach the defile, mounted elements overwatch their movement and provide direct-fire support from Strykers. The mortar 

**24 June 2025** 

**90** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**Offense** 

section can also provide indirect-fire support. Depending on the depth of the defile, the rifle squads may clear portions of the defile and call the Strykers forward to an intermediate position to continue to provide overwatch. The platoon leader considers the effectiveness of clearing a defile from within the low ground versus clearing one or both sides of the high ground that forms the defile. 

3-70. Once a defile has been cleared or seized, the dismounted Infantry can secure the terrain while the mounted elements bound forward. Once the mounted elements are set, the dismounted Infantry can once again push forward to clear the next defile. Clearing a defile is slow and deliberate, sacrificing speed. However, the clearance operation can maintain tempo with the goal of conserving combat power while achieving the mission. 

##### **DISMOUNT POINTS** 

3-71. The platoon leader will determine where the squads will dismount based on mission and terrain analysis and guidance from the company OPORD. DPs are typically behind the probable LC. DPs should be depicted on the graphical overlay and map. These DPs can be short of the objective, on the objective, or beyond the objective. Examples of dismount rehearsals include the following: 

- Stryker vehicles occupy covered and concealed positions. 

- Stryker VCs provide obscuration at the DP. 

- Stryker VCs relay tactical situation to dismounted Infantry leaders. 

- Stryker VCs provide orientation to the dismounting Infantry. 

- Rifle squad dismounts and clears forward or rearward of the Stryker. 

- Rifle squad deploys into team or squad formations to right or left side of the Stryker. 

- Platoon leader establishes C2 on the ground once dismounted. 

- Senior VC or other designated leader establishes C2 of the mounted element. 

###### **Short of the Objective** 

3-72. Dismounting squads prior to the probable LC has advantages. The advantages of dismounting the squads before reaching the objective are the protection of the Infantrymen during the dismount process, control at the DP, and the ability to continue suppression of the enemy by supporting indirect fires during the dismount. 

3-73. Dismounting prior to the objective allows the squads to clear antiarmor positions which will make conditions more favorable for the Strykers to maneuver onto the objective. The Infantrymen can also conduct dismount breaches while the Strykers overwatch in their SBF positions, enabling the Infantry squads to assault the objective. A disadvantage is the exposure of the squads to indirect and small-arms fires as they maneuver to the objective area and the possibility that suitable DPs will be targeted for enemy indirect fires. 

###### **On the Objective** 

3-74. Normally, Strykers will not dismount Infantry on the objective, unless the threat of enemy antiarmor has been eliminated. The primary advantages of dismounting on the objective are greater speed and enhanced protection of the squads as the platoon maneuvers to the objective area. There are some disadvantages to dismounting on the 

**24 June 2025** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**91** 

**Chapter 3** 

objective such as the difficulty in orienting the Infantry onto a specific location and the protection vulnerability of the Stryker (with and without security). 

###### **Beyond the Objective** 

3-75. Dismounting beyond the objective has several potential advantages such as effective controls at the DP, greater ease in orienting the dismounted elements to the terrain and the objectives of the assault, and possible disorientation of the enemy when they are forced to fight in an unexpected direction. At the same time, there are some significant disadvantages, such as the added complexity of attacking an enemy objective in-depth, Stryker vehicle vulnerability to short-range antiarmor systems, and increased risk of fratricide. 

##### **REMOUNT POINTS** 

3-76. The platoon leader identifies remount points for dismounted Infantry squads. The platoon leader will analyze the terrain and mission to determine the most suitable location for the dismounted Infantry squads to remount. Remount points are planned according to mission variables; however, dismounted Infantry may have to remount under fire. If necessary, they also may have to remount in the first available vehicle and then gain accountability prior to movement. Rehearsals of loading while under fire will reduce the risk of Soldiers not knowing what to do when approaching a Stryker with no room to remount. 

3-77. The platoon leader selects a remount point that permits the rapid loading of the dismounted element into the Strykers while minimizing both the dismounted Soldier’s and Stryker’s exposure to enemy fire (see figure 3-15). The platoon leader tries to locate the remount point as close as possible to the dismounted element. Squad leaders ensure that their Soldiers know the remount point location. When moving to the Strykers, the dismounted element ensures that they do not mask the Stryker’s fields of fire.

##### **FORMS OF MANEUVER** 

3-78. The platoon leader conducts maneuver through the synchronization of fire and movement. The platoon leader references the company OPORD for any dictated forms of maneuver and within the commander’s intent, the platoon leader selects a form of maneuver based on their analysis of the mission variables, METT-TC (I). The platoon leader achieves surprise by making unexpected maneuvers, rapidly changing tempo, avoiding observation, and using deceptive techniques and procedures. An operation may contain several forms of maneuver. The forms of maneuver are as follows: 

- Frontal attack. 

- Penetration 

- Envelopment. 

- Turning movement. 

- Infiltration. 

**_Note._** The Stryker is a support platform that provides mobility and firepower by when transporting the Infantry squad to a DP and then provides overwatch during movement. The Stryker is not a fighting vehicle. 

**24 June 2025**

**Chapter 3** 

###### **Frontal Attack** 

3-79. _Frontal attack_ is a form of maneuver in which an attacking force seeks to destroy a weaker enemy force or fix a larger enemy force in place over a broad front (FM 3-90). The frontal attack is the least advantageous to the platoon because it exposes the Stryker vehicle and dismounted Infantry to the concentrated fires of the enemy. The platoon normally conducts a frontal attack as part of a larger operation against a stationary or moving enemy force (see figure 3-16). 

3-80. Frontal attacks are executed with overwhelming and well-synchronized speed and strength against a weaker enemy. The platoon can execute a frontal attack when the enemy is at a clear and distinct disadvantage. The platoon leader should use supporting fires from the Stryker’s heavy weapons systems while doing so from a covered and concealed position well-short of the objective. 

3-81. Platoon leaders use graphical control measures to aid in briefing the platoon the plan. The platoon leader follows the graphical control measures received from the company OPORD and may not need to add more. The platoon leader can also use any other control measure necessary to control the front attack, including— 

- Attack positions. 

- LDs. 

- Phase lines. 

- Assault positions. 

- LOAs. 

- Directions of attack or axes of advance for every maneuver element. 

- SBF or ABF positions. 

- Direct fire control measures. 



**Figure 3-16. Frontal attack**

###### **Penetration** 

3-82. A _penetration_ is a form of maneuver in which a force attacks on a narrow front (FM 3-90). Penetrations are conducted when the enemy has no assailable flanks, enemy positions are overextended and weak spots are detected in the enemy defense, or time does not permit an envelopment. Penetrations are normally conducted at the battalion echelon and above. The Stryker Infantry rifle platoon may be utilized as a component of the assault, support, or might be part of a breach force in support of the penetration. Successful penetration depends on the attacking force’s ability to suppress enemy weapons systems, to concentrate forces to overwhelm the enemy defender at the point of penetration, and to pass sufficient forces through the point of breach (POB) to defeat the enemy quickly. (See FM 3-90 for more information.) 

###### **Envelopment** 

3-83. _Envelopment_ is a form of maneuver in which an attacking force avoids an enemy’s principal defense by attacking along an assailable flank (FM 3-90). At the tactical level, envelopments focus on seizing terrain, destroying specific enemy forces, and interdicting enemy withdrawal routes, but are also prepared to engage enemy forces repositioning within the objective, or enemy reserves or counterattacking forces (see figure 3-17). Generally, an envelopment is the preferred form of maneuver instead of a penetration or frontal attack because the attacking force tends to suffer fewer casualties while having the most opportunities to destroy the enemy. 



**Figure 3-17. Envelopment** 

###### **Turning Movement** 

3-84. A _turning movement_ is a form of maneuver in which the attacking force seeks to avoid the enemy’s principal defensive positions by attacking to the rear of their current positions forcing them to move or divert forces to meet the threat (FM 3-90). The objective of the turning movement is to make contact with the enemy, but at a location advantageous to the commander conducting the turning movement and out of the enemy’s established EA. 

3-85. A turning movement differs from envelopment because the force conducting a turning movement seeks to make the enemy forces displace from their current locations, 

**24 June 2025** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**95** 

**Chapter 3** 

whereas an enveloping force seeks to engage the enemy forces in their current locations from an unexpected direction. The platoon and company normally conduct a turning movement as part of a larger force, combined arms operation. 

###### **Infiltration** 

3-86. An _infiltration_ is a form of maneuver in which an attacking force conducts undetected movement through or into an area occupied by enemy forces (FM 3-90). Infiltration occurs by land, water, air, or a combination of means. Moving and assembling forces covertly through enemy positions is time consuming. To infiltrate successfully, the force avoids detection and engagement. Since this requirement limits the size and strength of the infiltrating force, the platoon leader is typically limited to the dismounted Infantry to conduct this form of maneuver. The platoon leader considers separate infiltration routes for the Strykers to control the noise and light discipline of the platoon. Infiltrated forces alone can rarely defeat an enemy. Infiltration is normally used in conjunction with other forms of maneuver. (See ATP 3-21.8 for more information.) 

#### **INTELLIGENCE** 

3-87. The platoon leader uses threat event templates, the SITEMP, the likely threat COA, the most dangerous threat COA, civil consideration products, terrain analysis, weather, and other intelligence products and assessments. The platoon leader can obtain this information from the battalion intelligence officer’s analysis and the company OPORD; however, the platoon leader must do the top-down analysis of higher products to understand elements unique to the platoon’s mission or assigned area. During offensive operations, platoon leaders should analyze terrain for impassable and slow go terrain. The evaluation of avenues of approach leads to a recommendation of the best avenues of approach to a command’s objective and to the identification of avenues of approach available to the threat for counterattack, withdrawal, or the movement of reinforcements or reserves. The leader also tries to determine the most advantageous area the enemy’s main defense might occupy, routes the enemy may use to conduct counterattacks, and other factors such as OAKOC. The attacking platoon continuously conducts information collection during the battle because it is unlikely the platoon leader has complete knowledge of the enemy’s intentions and actual actions. 

#### **FIRES** 

3-88. The platoon leader conducts fire support planning concurrently with the Stryker Infantry rifle company and Stryker Infantry battalion. The SBCT and Stryker Infantry battalion typically use top-down fire support planning, with bottom-up refinement of plans. As part of the top-down fire planning system, the company commander refines the fire support plan from higher headquarters to meet mission requirements, ensuring these refinements are incorporated into the higher headquarters’ plan. 

3-89. A clearly defined concept of fires enables the platoon leader and FO to articulate precisely how they want indirect fires to affect the enemy during the different phases of the operation. In turn, this allows the company FSO to facilitate the development of fires supporting accomplishment of the company’s mission down to the squad level. The commander will align enabler fires and dictate the type of fires to certain platoons. (See appendix B for more information.)

3-90. Prior to movement, the platoon leader plans for fires throughout the depth of the operation, specifically along the route to cover anticipated places of enemy contact, during actions on the objective, and during consolidate and reorganization activities. These planned targets are a product of the platoon leader’s analysis of the mission variables of METT-TC (I) and must be incorporated into the company’s fire support plan. 

#### **SUSTAINMENT** 

3-91. The objective of sustainment in offensive operations is to ensure the platoon maintains momentum. The platoon leader wants to take advantage of windows of opportunity and launch offensive operations with minimum advance warning time. The platoon sergeant and squad leaders must anticipate these events and maintain flexibility to support the offensive plan accordingly. 

3-92. _Sustainment_ is the provision of logistics, financial management, personnel services, and health service support necessary to maintain operations until successful mission completion (ADP 4-0). The platoon leader ensures they understand the company sustainment plan to facilitate the platoon’s sustainment during the operation. The platoon leader and platoon sergeant submit accurate quantities of their supply on hand to the company XO through the logistical status report. Higher headquarters determines when the logistics status is due and then the XO collects and submits platoon leader’s reports based on the assigned times. 

3-93. The platoon must be ready to refuel and rearm at any opportunity. Platoon sergeants must report consumption of Class III and Class V (see table 6-2 on page 292 for all classes of supplies) to the company during execution of the mission. The platoon is largely responsible for its own CASEVAC from the point of injury to the platoon and company CCP. CASEVAC can be either mounted (Stryker) or dismounted (litter carry), depending on the distance from the point of injury to the CCP. 

3-94. An important aspect of sustainment in a Stryker Infantry rifle platoon is executed by the field maintenance team (FMT). The platoon leader ensures their platoon conducts the proper preventive maintenance checks and services (PMCS) throughout an operation. Thorough PMCS by the operators allows the FMT to order the correct parts to ensure the Strykers maintain a fully mission-capable status. (See ATP 3-21.11 for more information on sustainment.) 

#### **PROTECTION** 

3-95. The rapid tempo and changing nature of the offense presents challenges to the protection of friendly assets. _Protection_ is the preservation of the effectiveness and survivability of mission-related military and nonmilitary personnel, equipment, facilities, information, and infrastructure deployed or located within or outside the boundaries of a given operational area (JP 3-0). The platoon leader will extract the information needed on protection from the company and battalion OPORDs. If applicable the platoon leader coordinates with their higher headquarters for additional protection resources needed to achieve mission success. 

3-96. Denying the enemy, a chance to plan, prepare, and execute a response to the friendly offense by maintaining a high operational tempo is a vital means the leader 

**24 June 2025** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**97** 

**Chapter 3** 

employs to ensure the survivability of the platoon. The forward movement of subordinate units is critical if the leader is to maintain the initiative necessary for offensive operations. Using multiple routes, wise use of terrain, dispersion, scheduled rotations, and relief of forces before they culminate are techniques for maintaining a high tempo of offense. 

3-97. Obscuration reduces the enemy’s visibility and enhances protection. Obscurants reduce the ability of the enemy to deliver effective fires, to hamper hostile operations, and to deny the enemy information on friendly positions and maneuvers. As an example, leaders integrate and synchronize the use of obscurations to support critical actions such during breaching or assaults. The mission variables of METT-TC (I) determine the exact techniques employed in a specific situation. 

3-98. Depending on the threat, primary protection concerns of the platoon leader may be enemy air threats, to include hostile sUASs. (See drill 07-PLT-D8015, appendix C.) If these threats exist, the leader prepares the unit and adjusts the scheme of maneuver accordingly. In the face of an enemy air threat, the platoon usually has minimal active and passive (with its organic weapons) air defenses. Air defense units are usually not assigned below SBCT level. However, air defense assets may be located near the platoon and may provide coverage. If air defense elements are assigned, the platoon leader with the advisement of the air defense element leader determines likely enemy air avenues of approach and plans movement routes accordingly. The platoon leader establishes priorities for protection during movement and during actions on the objective. (See ATP 3-01.81 for more information on counter-unmanned aircraft system [C-UAS] techniques.) 

3-99. Planning for air defense and implementing all forms of active and passive air defense measures are imperative to minimize the vulnerability to enemy air attack. The platoon leader integrates the fire support plan with any attached or supporting air defense assets. Should hostile aircraft attack during movement, the subordinate unit under attack moves off the road into a defensive posture and immediately engages the aircraft with all available automatic weapons. The rest of the platoon moves to covered and concealed areas until the engagement ends. Air defense units, when available, may move with the platoon. In this case, the air defense unit leader ensures both the current and projected weapons control status (WCS) and air defense warning are known. (See ATP 3-01.8 for additional information.) 

3-100. In the offense, _survivability operations_ , those military activities that alter the physical environment to provide or improve cover, camouflage, and concealment (ATP 3-37.34), enhance the ability to avoid or withstand hostile actions by altering the physical environment. _Survivability_ is the quality or capability of military forces which permits them to avoid or withstand hostile actions or environmental conditions while retaining the ability to fulfill their primary mission (ATP 3-37.34). Protective hasty fighting positions or indirect fire survivability positions may be required in the offense. When dig assets are unavailable, the platoon still uses the micro-terrain to achieve protection effects, and exclusively so during the offense. Camouflage and concealment typically play a greater role in survivability during offensive operations. The platoon can avoid being targeted by UAS and loitering munitions by moving through the tree lines, maintaining dispersion, and reducing their thermal signature. The use of terrain provides a measure of protection during halts in the advance, but the platoon should

develop as many protective measures as necessary for key weapons systems, command posts, and critical supplies. Some examples are the following: 

- Reduce personnel, vehicle, thermal, and electronic signatures using camouflage. 

- Use dispersion in movement formations. 

- Conduct electromagnetic protection. 

- Emplace air guards. 

- Plan and execute survivability-moves. 

- Train and rehearse battle drills for all forms of contact, to include CBRN. 

3-101. The platoon leader integrates considerations for operating in CBRN environments into offensive planning depending on the CBRN threat. CBRN considerations include the following: 

- Understand enemy CBRN threat capabilities. 

- Employ organic CBRN capabilities to maximize protection across the platoon. 

- Understand the conditions to recognize and react to a CBRN incident. 

- Disseminate information regarding observed CBRN threats or hazards to the platoon immediately, send report to higher. 

- Understand duration of protection gear effectiveness. 

- Ensure Soldiers have necessary medical countermeasures (such as antidote treatment nerve agent auto-injector) and decontamination kits. 

- Develop decontamination plans based on the platoon leader’s priorities and vulnerability assessment. 

- Disseminate information regarding planned and active decontamination sites. 

- Prepare to conduct CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance (normally conducted by the scout platoon) to protect the force and enable freedom of maneuver. 

3-102. The personal protective equipment posture provides a threat-based framework for commanders and subordinate leaders to determine the optimal level of body armor and personal protective equipment Soldiers need to wear while conducting an operation. The mission-oriented protective posture (MOPP) levels range from MOPP 0 to MOPP 4 based on the operation and assessed CBRN threats on the battlefield. (See ATP 3-21.18 for a detailed discussion.) 

3-103. The most basic protection from enemy EW is radio discipline. This can take the form of limiting transmissions, antenna masking, and use of low power. Limiting the number of overall transmissions and transmission time when a radio microphone is keyed makes enemy EW operators’ targeting of friendly forces for geolocation and jamming more difficult. 

3-104. Detainees and captured enemy equipment or materiel often provide excellent combat information. This information is of tactical value only if the platoon processes and evacuates detainees and materiel to the rear quickly. In all tactical situations, the platoon will have specific procedures and guidelines for processing detainees and captured materiel. 

3-105. As a matter of policy, all detainees are treated as enemy prisoners of war until their appropriate legal status is determined by a competent authority according to the criteria enumerated in the Geneva Convention Relatives to the Treatment of Prisoners 

**24 June 2025** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**99** 

**Chapter 3** 

of War. However, as a practical matter, when a platoon captures enemy personnel, they must provide the initial processing and holding for detainees. Detainee processing is a resource-intensive and politically sensitive operation requiring detailed training, guidance, and supervision. 

3-106. All detainees immediately shall be given humanitarian care and treatment. U.S. Armed Forces never will torture, maltreat, or purposely place detained persons in positions of danger. There is never a military necessity exception to violate these principles. 

3-107. Soldiers must process detainees using the “search, silence, segregate, speed, safeguard, and tag” (5 Ss and T) technique. The steps are noted in paragraphs 3-108 through 3-116. 

##### **SEARCH** 

3-108. To perform the search, neutralize a detainee and confiscate weapons, personal items, and items of potential intelligence or evidentiary value. 

##### **SILENCE** 

3-109. Prevent detainees from communicating with one another or making audible clamor. Silence uncooperative detainees by muffling them with a soft, clean cloth tied around their mouths and fastened at the backs of their heads. Neither use duct tape or other adhesives, nor place a cloth or objects inside the mouth, nor apply physical force to silence detainees. 

##### **SEGREGATE** 

3-110. Segregate detainees according to policy and SOPs. (Segregation requirements differ from operation to operation.) The ability to segregate detainees may be limited by the availability of manpower and resources at the point of contact. At a minimum, try to segregate detainees by grade, gender, age (keeping adults from juveniles and small children with mothers), and security risk. Military intelligence and military police personnel can provide additional guidance and support in determining the appropriate segregation criteria. 

##### **SAFEGUARD** 

3-111. Protect detainees and ensure the custody and integrity of all confiscated items. Soldiers must safeguard detainees from combat risk, harm caused by other detainees, and improper treatment or care. Report all injuries. Correct and report violations of U.S. military policy that occur while safeguarding detainees. Acts, omissions, or both that constitute inhumane treatment are violations of the law of armed conflict and, as such, must be corrected immediately. Simply reporting violations is insufficient. If a violation is ongoing, a Soldier has an obligation to stop the violation and report it. 

##### **SPEED TO A SAFE AREA/REAR** 

3-112. Quickly move detainees from the continuing risks associated with other combatants or sympathizers who still may be in the area of capture. If there are more detainees than the Soldiers can control, call for additional support, search the detainees, and hold them in place until reinforcements arrive. Evacuate detainees from the

**Offense** 

battlefield to a holding area or facility as soon as possible. Transfer captured documents and other property to the forces assuming responsibility of the detainees. 

##### **TAG** 

3-113. Ensure that each detainee is tagged using DD Form 2745 ( _Enemy Prisoner of War [EPW] Capture Tag_ ). Confiscated equipment, personal items, and evidence will be linked to the detainee using the DD Form 2745 number. When a DA Form 4137 ( _Evidence/Property Custody Document_ ) is used to document confiscated items, it will be linked to the detainee by annotating the DD Form 2745 control number on the form or by field expedient means. Field expedient means should include tagging with date and time of capture, location of capture, capturing unit, and circumstances of capture. There are three parts to this form. DD Form 2745, Unit Record Card, Part B, is the unit record copy. DD Form 2745, Document/Special Equipment Weapons Card, Part C, is for detainee confiscated property. Tagging is critical. If it does not happen, the ability of higher headquarters to obtain pertinent tactical information quickly is reduced greatly. 

3-114. Soldiers capturing equipment, documents, and detainees should tag them (using the DD Form 2745, Part A), take digital pictures, and report the capture immediately. Detainees are allowed to keep individual protective equipment such as a protective mask. (See FM 3-63 for additional information.) 

3-115. Detainees should be evacuated as soon as is practical to the higher echelon detainee collection point. Military police teams, when attached, can assist in the rapid evacuation of detainees to these collection points. Tactical questioning of detainees is allowed relative to collection of commander’s critical information requirements. However, detainees must always be treated in accordance with Department of Defense (DOD) programs and policies that ensure compliance with the laws of the United States; the law of armed conflict, including the Geneva Conventions, and humane treatment during all intelligence interrogations, detainee debriefings, or tactical questioning. (See DOD Directive 2310.01E, DOD Directive 3115.09, and DOD Directive 2311.01.) 

3-116. The platoon leader protects subordinate elements to deny the enemy the capability to interfere with their ongoing operations. Protection also meets the leader’s legal and moral obligations to the organization’s Soldiers. Additional protection tasks conducted by the platoon in the offense may include: 

- Employing safety techniques (including avoiding _fratricide_ —the unintentional killing or wounding of friendly or neutral personnel by friendly firepower [ADP 3-37]). 

- Implementing _operations security_ —an activity that identifies and controls critical information and indicators of friendly force actions (JP 3-55). 

- Implementing _physical security_ —that part of security concerned with physical measures designed to safeguard personnel; to prevent unauthorized access to equipment, installations, material, and documents; and to safeguard them against espionage, sabotage, damage, and theft (JP 3-0).

##### **SECTION III – ACTIONS ON CONTACT** 

3-117. _Actions on contact_ is a process to help leaders understand what is happening and to take action (FM 3-90). Actions on contact-is a process to help leaders understand what is happening and to take action. Leaders analyze the enemy throughout TLP to identify all likely contact situations that may occur during an operation and consider their initial actions. Analysis of the enemy will identify many areas where enemy contact is likely, however it will not identify all of them. The framework for taking actions on contact should guide all enemy contact, whether anticipated or not. Actions on contact does not replace the use of battle drills; instead, battle drills may be elements of the broader process of taking actions on contact. Battle drills are the actions of individual Soldiers and small units when they meet the enemy (see appendix C for battle drills). 

3-118. Typically, a unit’s SOP dictates specific actions, to include battle drills and reports, depending on the type of contact. Additionally, the mission variables, commander’s intent and guidance, and scheme of maneuver guide the actions individual units take when they make enemy contact. 

3-119. During movement, once the lead element of a force (for example, during the conduct of a movement to contact) encounters an enemy, they conduct actions on contact. Obstacles encountered during movement are treated like enemy contact, in that, the unit assumes the obstacles are covered by fire. Once contact with the enemy is made, squads and platoons execute the appropriate actions on contact, and leaders begin to maneuver their units. The unit’s security force will then seek to gain a tactical advantage over an enemy by using tempo and initiative to conduct these actions, allowing it to gain and maintain contact without becoming decisively engaged, a fully committed force or unit that cannot maneuver or extricate itself (see FM 3-90). How quickly the unit develops the situation is directly related to its security, and the tempo is directly related to the unit’s use of well-rehearsed tactical SOP and battle drills. The platoon’s proficiency with both their tactical SOP and battle drills will allow them to survive contact by executing at a high tempo, allowing them to dominate a situation and regain the initiative. 

#### **FOUR STEPS OF ACTIONS ON CONTACT** 

3-120. The steps of actions on contact are not intended to generate a rigid, lockstep response to the enemy. Rather, the goal is to provide an orderly framework that gives leaders and soldiers a process to survive the initial contact and organize their subsequent actions. When applied, many of the actions may happen simultaneously. Unit leaders must apply timely actions and sound decision making when applying the steps. Actions on contact are applicable to all types of operations. They are just as applicable to a squad coming into direct fire contact with an enemy during a movement to contact, an armor company observing enemy in the defense, a signal element ambushed by the enemy, or a division in the attack. This framework is a way for leaders to quickly determine if things are going according to plan and what actions they need to take to either stay on plan or adjust to the new situation. (See FM 3-90 for more information.) 

**24 June 2025** 

**102** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**Offense** 

3-121. Stryker Infantry platoons and squads execute actions on contact using a logical, well-organized process of decision making and action entailing these four steps: 

- React. 

- Develop the situation. 

- Choose an action. 

- Execute and report. 

##### **REACT** 

3-122. If the enemy initiates the contact, the element in contact conducts the react to contact battle drill. This immediate action deploys the platoon into a new formation or takes other necessary actions to survive contact or posture the platoon to develop the situation. Two fundamental considerations related to survivability are the platoon’s actions and the platoon leaders’ decisions during every reaction to contact. First, does the platoon stay mounted or (remount); or do squads dismount or stay dismounted. Second, does the platoon stay in place or does it displace or otherwise break contact? 

3-123. Any unengaged element monitors the situation and prepares to either support the portion of the platoon in contact or continue the mission. Simultaneously, the platoon, mounted element, or squad in contact reports the contact to their higher headquarters which helps them to develop the situation. This also alerts the higher echelon and allows the initiation of necessary actions. Higher headquarters will monitor and provide support through resources or maneuver to assist in the development of the situation. 

3-124. If friendly forces make contact first without the enemy being aware, they determine if they have been detected, if not they move to a location where they will not be observed and continue the actions on contact process. The Stryker Infantry rifle platoon should attempt to make contact with the smallest element possible—even an unmanned system. This element is the one that reacts to contact, while the rest of the force begins conducting actions on contact at different tempos. 

##### **DEVELOP THE SITUATION** 

3-125. After initial actions to survive contact, the leader develops the situation to define the threat. This includes all necessary steps to better understand the strength (superior or inferior), nature, location and disposition, and capabilities of threat forces in contact. The leader may employ both direct and indirect fires while maneuvering the platoon to gain understanding. While developing the situation, it is critical the platoon is not fixed by enemy fires to retain freedom of maneuver and provide flexibility in maneuver options for the platoon leader or company commander. The platoon leader’s goals in developing the situation are first survival, then depending on the nature of contact, to deliver an overwhelming response, then to regain the initiative. The platoon leader considers whether the type and nature of contact will require the platoon to deviate from the current plan. While formulating possible courses of action, the platoon leader considers risk to force, risk to mission, and whether there are emerging opportunities. 

3-126. The unit in contact develops the situation to define the threat being faced. This helps to develop the situation across the front of the unit and ultimately provides more maneuver space to execute further actions. The unit in contact initiates direct and indirect fires to develop the situation, gain initiative and compare courses of action. As the situation develops and the enemy force’s dispositions, strength, and intentions 

**24 June 2025** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**103** 

**Chapter 3** 

become clearer, the unit in contact submits additional reports. Typical things to consider include, but are not limited to— 

- Size, activity, location, composition, and orientation of the enemy force. 

- Understanding of enemy capabilities with respect to friendly forces (superior or inferior enemy force) 

- Identification of enemy flanks and whether they are assailable. 

- Impact of obstacles and terrain. 

- Enemy capabilities. 

- Probable enemy intentions. 

- Potential methods of gaining positional advantage over the enemy. 

- Friendly situation (location, strength, and capabilities). 

- Possible friendly actions to achieve the specified end state. 

- Means of presenting the enemy with multiple dilemmas. 

3-127. For lower echelons with a small frontage such as platoons and below, it will not take long to develop the situation. Additional considerations should include views from UASs, employment of mortars and artillery, and recon by fire. 

##### **CHOOSE AN ACTION** 

3-128. After the platoon makes contact, the platoon leader gathers information to make an assessment based on their understanding of the enemy and friendly forces’ composition and disposition and chooses an action consistent with the higher echelon commander’s intent and within the unit’s capabilities. These actions typically are— 

- Attack. 

- Bypass. 

- Defend. 

- Delay. 

- Withdrawal. 

- Establish ABF or SBF in support of company maneuver. 

- Additional considerations are breach and break contact. 

3-129. Some actions require the company commanders’ approval prior to execution. Reasons for needing a higher commander’s approval could include the following: 

- Action requires additional resources. 

- Action consumes scarce, limited, or otherwise mission-essential resources, such as breaching assets. 

- Action is not within the commander’s intent. 

- Action sets conditions for the higher echelon to continue. 

- Action commits the company commander to a changed scheme of maneuver. 

##### **EXECUTE AND REPORT** 

3-130. With the action selected and, if needed, approved by their higher echelon, the unit in contact takes the appropriate actions. If the action is to attack, the unit in contact immediately attacks if it has sufficient, immediately available combat power to overwhelm the enemy force. If the action is to defend or withdraw, to disengage from an enemy force and move in a direction away from the enemy (see ADP 3-90), the unit in contact does so while maintaining contact and continuing to gain as much information

as possible about the enemy forces disposition and positions. If the action is to bypass the enemy, the unit in contact maintains contact and continues their mission. Unless specifically told by their higher headquarters to break contact, the unit in contact will maintain contact no matter which action is chosen. Regardless of the chosen action, reporting to the next higher echelon is required to ensure the unit is staying within the commander’s intent. If maneuvering as part of the company, the platoon will often be directed to establish an ABF or SBF position to enable the company to maneuver. 

#### **FORMS OF CONTACT** 

3-131. In offensive and defensive operations, contact occurs when the Stryker Infantry rifle platoon encounters a situation requiring a lethal or nonlethal response to the enemy. (See FM 3-90 for more information.) Such forms of contact may entail one or more of the following types of interactions described in paragraphs 3-132 through 3-140. 

##### **DIRECT** 

3-132. Direct forms of contact include interactions from ground-based, line-of-sight weapons systems (small arms, tank main guns, and AT missiles). 

##### **INDIRECT** 

3-133. Indirect forms of contact are interactions from no line-of-sight weapons systems (including cannon artillery, mortars, and rockets). 

##### **NONHOSTILE** 

3-134. Nonhostile contact includes neutral interactions that may degrade military operations (including civilians on the battlefield, nongovernmental organizations, or neutral forces). 

##### **OBSTACLES** 

3-135. Obstacles include interactions from natural and manmade obstacles (including rivers and minefields). 

##### **CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL, AND NUCLEAR** 

3-136. CBRN includes interactions from friendly, enemy, and civilian CBRN effects (including chemical attacks, nuclear attacks, industrial accidents, and toxic or hazardous materiel). 

##### **AERIAL** 

3-137. Aerial forms of contact include interactions from air-based combat platforms (including attack helicopters, armed or unarmed UAS, and fixed-wing aircraft). 

##### **VISUAL** 

3-138. Visual contact includes interactions from acquisition via the human eye, optical, or electro-optical systems (including ground reconnaissance, telescopic, thermal, and IR sights on weapons and sensor platforms such as UAS and satellites).

**105** 

**Chapter 3** 

##### **ELECTROMAGNETIC** 

3-139. Electromagnetic forms of contact include interactions via systems used to acquire, degrade, or destroy using select portions of the electromagnetic spectrum (including radar systems, jamming, cyberspace, and electromagnetic pulse). 

##### **INFLUENCE** 

3-140. Influence includes interactions through the information dimension intended to shape the perceptions, behaviors, and decision making of people relative to a policy or military objective (including through social media, telecommunications, human interaction, and other forms of communication and contact). 

##### **SECTION IV – MOVEMENT TO CONTACT** 

3-141. _Movement to contact_ is a type of offensive operation designed to establish or gain contact to develop the situation (FM 3-90). It ends when enemy contact is made or upon arrival at a designated march objective or other control measure such as a phase line or LOA. The platoon usually conducts movement to contact as part of an Infantry rifle company or larger element. Based upon the mission variables of METT-TC (I), the platoon may conduct the operation independently. Search and attack, and cordon and search are variations of a movement to contact. 

**_Note._** In an environment focused on low-intensity conflict or stability operations, the platoon typically operates under more restrictive ROE and will typically conduct either a cordon and search or search and attack when conducting a movement to contact. _Cordon and search_ is a variation of movement to contact where a friendly force isolates and searches a target area (FM 3-90). _Search and attack_ is variation of a movement to contact where a friendly force conducts coordinated attacks to defeat a distributed enemy force (FM 3-90). (See ATP 3-21.11 and ATP 3-21.21 for a detailed discussion of each subordinate variation.) 

3-142. The platoon may participate in a movement to contact in a variety of circumstances when the enemy situation is not clear. The platoon may participate in a movement to contact when— 

- Attacking to straighten the front-line trace. 

- Conducting operations within the enemy’s security zone. 

- Following an enemy force that has rapidly displaced. 

- Restrictive terrain allows considerable concealment to threat forces. 

- Occupying security positions such as a screen line or counterreconnaissance positions. 

#### **CONDUCT OF MOVEMENT TO CONTACT** 

3-143. Purposeful and aggressive movement, decentralized control, and hasty deployment of formations from the march to conduct offensive operations characterize the movement to contact. The fundamentals of movement to contact are— 

- Focusing all efforts on finding the enemy. 

**24 June 2025** 

**106** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**Offense** 

- Making initial contact with the smallest force possible, consistent with protecting the force. 

- Making initial contact with small, mobile, self-contained forces, including unmanned systems. 

   - Such contact avoids decisive engagement of the main body on ground chosen by the enemy. 

   - This allows the leader maximum flexibility to develop the situation. 

- Task-organizing the force and uses movement formations to deploy and attack rapidly in all directions. 

- Keeping subordinate forces within supporting distances to facilitate a flexible response. 

- Maintaining contact regardless of the COA adopted once contact is made. 

#### **ORGANIZATION OF FORCES** 

3-144. The Stryker Infantry rifle platoon normally conducts movement to contact as part of a company within the battalion; however, based on the mission variables of METT-TC (I) it can conduct the operation independently. The platoon leader analyzes the situation and selects the proper movement formation and movement technique to conduct the mission. The leader reports all information rapidly and accurately and strives to gain and maintain contact with the enemy. The platoon leader retains freedom of maneuver by moving the platoon in a manner that— 

- Employs a movement formation and technique that keeps the bulk of the platoon out of contact and able to maneuver when making contact. 

- Rapidly develops the situation to gain understanding of the disposition of threat forces. 

- Ensures continuous, effective overwatch of moving elements. 

- Ensures the platoon’s elements are not fixed in position by enemy fires. 

- Gains fire superiority when in contact to suppress enemy forces. 

3-145. Movement to contact is organized as a minimum with a forward security force, (either a covering force or an advance guard), and a main body. The reserve, fires, engineer, and sustainment assets if available are included in the main body. Based on METT-TC (I), the leader may increase the unit’s security by resourcing an offensive covering force and an advance guard for each column, as well as flank and rear security. This is normally a screen or guard. A _screen_ is a type of security operation that primarily provides early warning to the protected force (ADP 3-90). A _guard_ is a type of security operation done to protect the main body by fighting to gain time while preventing enemy ground observation of and direct fire against the main body (ADP 3-90). The platoon would be organized into one of the following forces when conducting a movement to contact as part of a larger force. 

##### **SECURITY FORCES** 

3-146. The primary purpose to this organization is the early and accurate reporting it provides on the enemy and terrain. Depth is essential for providing early warning and reaction time to leaders at the platoon, company, and battalion levels. It enables leaders to conduct actions on contact, preserving the parent unit’s freedom of movement and maneuver.

##### **ADVANCE GUARD** 

3-147. When the platoon serves as the advance guard, its purpose is to protect the main body from surprise attack and develop the situation to protect the deployment of the main body when it is committed to action. These responsibilities include the following: 

- Providing security and early warning for the main body and facilitating its uninterrupted advance. 

- Conducting reconnaissance to locate enemy forces within the command directed boundaries and along the platoons’ axis of advance. 

- Conducting actions on contact to retain freedom of maneuver for the unit. 

- Calling for indirect fires to impede or harass the enemy. 

- Destroying enemy reconnaissance elements. 

- Finding, fixing, defeating, destroying, or containing enemy security forces to retain freedom of maneuver for the unit. 

- Bypassing and reporting obstacles or acting as the support or breach force during breaching operations. 

3-148. Composition of the advance guard depends upon METT-TC (I). In open terrain, it may move mounted but in restricted, close, complex, or urban terrain, dismounted movement with Strykers in the overwatch may be a better choice. Engineers and tanks may be attached to the advance guard. The mortar platoon or a mortar section may support the advance guard. 

3-149. The advance guard is the commander’s main effort and should be designated as the priority for fires, and all other forms of support. Once the main body is committed, priorities will shift to that element. In planning the movement to contact, each decision point should be based on the actions of the advance guard. 

##### **FLANK GUARD** 

3-150. The platoon can provide a moving flank screen under company control. This is done through formation selection. Normally, this element conducts a moving flank screen using alternating or successive bounds with squads and mounted elements. These elements remain at a distance from the main body, allowing the battalion time and space to maneuver to either flank. Flank security elements operate far enough out to prevent the enemy from surprising the main body with direct fires. Indirect fires are planned on major flank approaches to enhance security. 

##### **REAR GUARD** 

3-151. The platoon may provide rear security, but combat forces are not normally available to perform this mission. The battalion provides its own rear security, assisted by rapid forward movement, which gives the enemy less opportunity to react or reposition forces to attack. Upon switching from a movement to contact to an attack, the platoon normally conducts follow and support of the main body. 

##### **MAIN BODY** 

3-152. The _main body_ is the principal part of a tactical command or formation. It does not include detached elements of the command, such as advance guards, flank guards, and covering forces (ADP 3-90). The combat elements of the main body are prepared to 

**24 June 2025** 

**108** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**Offense** 

deploy and maneuver rapidly to a decisive point on the battlefield to destroy the enemy. The main body bases its movement on the advance guard. The main body, remaining attuned to the advance guard’s situation, provides responsive support when the advance guard makes contact. Tasks the platoon can perform within the main body include the following: 

- Finding, fixing, defeating, destroying, or containing the enemy’s fixing force followed by the enemy assault force or site exploitation force, to retain freedom of maneuver for the remainder of the company team. 

- Maneuvering to develop the situation and gain understanding of enemy capabilities and disposition. 

- Executing a COA to defeat or destroy a designated enemy main body element. 

- Standard formations and battle drills that allow the commander to shift combat power rapidly. 

- Based on their knowledge of commander’s intent and their own situational awareness, platoon leaders anticipate the commander’s decisions for commitment of the main body and plan accordingly. 

- Reconstitute the battalion reserve force, when ready. 

3-153. Standard formations and battle drills allows the commander to shift combat power rapidly. Platoons and squads employ the appropriate movement techniques within the company formation. Leaders, based on their knowledge of commander’s intent and their own situational awareness, anticipate decisions for commitment of the main body and plan accordingly. 

##### **RESERVE** 

3-154. The Stryker Infantry rifle platoon may be identified as part of the battalion reserve. The platoon itself does not have a reserve. The mission variables determine the size of the reserve, and the more unknown the enemy situation, the larger the size of the reserve. On contact with enemy forces, a reserve provides flexibility to react to unforeseen circumstances and allows a unit to resume its movement. 

#### **CONTROL MEASURES** 

3-155. Execution of a movement to contact usually starts from an LD at the time specified in the OPORD. The unit’s movement is controlled by phase lines, contact points, and checkpoints as required (see figure 3-18 on page 110). The depth of the movement to contact is usually controlled by a _limit of advance—_ a phase line used to control forward progress of the attack (ADP 3-90) or a _forward boundary_ —a boundary that delineates the forward edge of a unit’s area of operation (FM 3-90). A _lateral boundary_ is a boundary defining the left or right limit of a unit’s assigned area (FM 3-90). One or more objectives are designated to limit the extent of the movement to contact and to orient the force. However, these are often terrain-oriented (commonly called march objectives) and used only to guide movement. Although movement to contact may result in taking a terrain objective, the primary focus should be on the enemy force. The leader can designate a series of phase lines successively becoming the new _rear boundary—_ a boundary that delineates the rearward limits of a unit’s assigned area (FM 3-90) of forward security elements as the force advances. Each rear boundary becomes the forward boundary of the main body and shifts as the security force moves

forward. The rear boundary of the main body designates the limit of responsibility of the rear security element. This line also shifts as the main body moves forward. The platoon leader should develop and nest their graphic control measures with their commander. When enough information is available to locate a significant enemy force(s), then another type of offensive operation (for example, an attack) should be conducted. (See FM 3-90 for a detailed discussion.)

#### **PLAN** 

3-156. As in any type of operation, the platoon leader plans to focus operations on finding the enemy and then delaying, disrupting, and destroying each enemy force as much as possible before direct-fire range. In movement to contact, the goal is to prevent a meeting engagement with the enemy. A _meeting engagement_ is a combat action that occurs when a moving force engages an enemy at an unexpected time and place (FM 3-90). Units plan and conduct movement to contact to gain or regain contact with the enemy. The movement to contact ends at a defined stopping point such as the LOA, march objective, or when they transition to a different operation, or when they make contact. 

3-157. Planning begins by developing the concept of the operations with the focus on controlling the objective and conducting a reverse planning sequence from the objective to the LD. This is accomplished by understanding the commander’s intent and developing a simple concept of operations. The platoon leader receives guidance from the commander on the PIRs and develops a plan to answer the commander’s PIR. To plan the mission, the platoon leader must understand the breadth and depth of the axis of advance, whether there are any established bypass criteria, and the required effects to be achieved against all enemy forces in zone. _Bypass criteria_ are the measures 

**24 June 2025** 

**110** 

**ATP 3-21.9** 

**Offense** 

established by higher echelon headquarters that specify the conditions and size under which enemy units and contact may be avoided (FM 3-90). 

3-158. The platoon leader must have a good indirect fire plan for their route to cover anticipated places of contact. They work with the company FSO and FOs to develop the platoon’s fire plan. These targets are a product of the platoon leader’s analysis of the factors of METT-TC (I) and must incorporate the platoon’s fire plan into the company indirect fire plan. The platoon leader, platoon sergeant, squad leaders, and mounted leaders may initiate the calls for fire. 

3-159. When planning, the platoon leader identifies where the platoon will likely transition from movement to maneuver. This will allow the platoon leader to decide which movement formations will be most effective against suspected enemy forces. They plan to make enemy contact with the smallest friendly force possible, preferably an UAS or sensor. This allows the platoon leader sufficient time, space, and uncommitted combat power to maneuver and develop the situation for the company commander. 

3-160. Leaders conduct information collection to determine the enemy’s location and intent while conducting security operations to protect the main body. Information collection includes available manned and unmanned aircraft assets and Soldier-borne sensors, allowing the main body to focus on planning and preparation. Platoon leaders use all available information and intelligence to identify the probable locations for meeting engagements. The platoon should conduct rehearsals on hasty attack, bypass maneuvers, and hasty defenses. Platoon leaders also identify other forms of contact, by type and location, anticipates associated actions, and battle drills. 

3-161. The platoon leader develops contingency plans in the case of meeting an unexpected enemy force or obstacle. They develop options during their planning. Contingency plans may consist of the following actions: 

- What are platoon’s actions if they make contact with a small enemy force? 

- What are the platoon’s actions if they make contact with a larger force beyond its capabilities to defeat? 

- What are the platoon’s actions if they make contact with an obstacle unidentified by higher? 

- Action to report and bypass an enemy force. 

- Maneuver options and transitions. 

#### **PREPARE** 

3-162. During preparation for the mission and prior to LD, the platoon receives intelligence updates and incorporates the intelligence into the plan. The platoon leader receives the intelligence updates from the commander and the battalion’s intelligence section cell. The platoon leader should also request any updated imagery from higher headquarters to develop situational awareness and make any adjustments to the final plan. The platoon leader communicates any changes in enemy intelligence to their subordinates and receives a backbrief to confirm their understanding. 

3-163. The platoon leader must ensure subordinates understand the company commander’s intent and concept of operations and the platoon’s concept of operations and platoon’s intent, in addition to their individual missions even as new information

becomes available. The platoon leader uses confirmation briefs, backbriefs, and rehearsals to ensure missions are understood and all actions are integrated and synchronized. Simple plans that are flexible and rehearsed repetitively against various enemy conditions and that rely on established tactical SOPs are essential to success. 

3-164. The platoon leader seeks to rehearse the operation from initiation to occupation of the final march objective or LOA. Rehearsals include decision points and actions taken upon each decision. Often, the platoon leader prioritizes maneuver options and enemy COAs to be rehearsed based on the time available. The rehearsal focuses on locating the enemy, developing the situation, executing transition to a maneuver option, exercising direct and indirect fire control measures, and exploiting success. The rehearsal must consider the potential of encountering stationary or moving enemy forces. (See chapter 2 for more information on preparation activities, specifically inspections.) Other actions to consider during rehearsals include the following: 

- Uncoil from the AA and movement from current positions. 

- Routes (passage points, contact points, checkpoints, and CCP). 

- Forward passage of lines. 

- Movement formations, movement techniques. 

- Mounted sectors of fire, gun tube orientation and direct fire control measures.
